title: Before Seeking a Win-Win Compromise, Go for a Total-Win Solution
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article critiques the Win-Win negotiation ideal, arguing that most win-win outcomes actually rely on compromise, and compromise tends to breed resentment because sacrifices are rarely perceived as equally shared. It introduces a 'Total-Win' alternative, which seeks a genuinely new solution advancing both parties' most important goals without either side feeling they gave anything up. The piece is candid that Total-Win outcomes are hard to reach and require challenging both sides' starting assumptions, but argues that even attempting one reveals possibilities a purely compromise-oriented negotiation would miss.
points: Win-Win outcomes are critiqued as usually requiring compromise, which breeds resentment over time.
A 'Total-Win' alternative seeks a genuinely new solution that advances both parties' key goals without concessions.
Total-Win requires challenging both sides' starting assumptions and is described as never easy to reach.
Even attempting a Total-Win, the article argues, reveals possibilities compromise-focused negotiation misses.
quotes: Instead of pursuing a win-lose outcome where one party achieves more than the other, decision-making and negotiation experts push the idea of achieving a Win-Win resolution whereby both parties benefit.
Win-Win solutions almost always require concessions on the part of both sides.
But once the solution is put into action, concessions can lead to feelings of resentment, dissatisfaction, and frustration, as sacrifices are seldom perceived to be equally shared.
A Total-Win negotiation stresses the creation of innovative solutions that generate the maximum value for both parties.
When leaders limit themselves to choices that seem reasonable and practical, they often disconnect themselves from what is possible.
